text.title: Retainer Pricing Methodology Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every Retainer Pricing Methodology application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The decision MUST name exactly one retainer shape and its defining term: block-of-hours (prepaid hours per month, rollover policy, overage rate), outcome-based (a fixed list of deliverables per period), or availability (reserved capacity with a response-time commitment and a stated maximum monthly load). A hybrid is allowed only if the artefact states which shape governs invoicing and which clause governs scope disputes.

rationale.source: Jonathan Stark, Hourly Billing Is Nuts (2016) and writing on productized retainers; Brennan Dunn, Double Your Freelancing Rate

rule.rationale: "Retainer" without a shape is an hourly contract with a deposit, and the client will read it as the shape most favourable to them: unlimited availability at a block-of-hours price. Naming the shape is what makes the scope clause enforceable and the price defensible when the 60-hour month arrives.

rule.statement: The monthly retainer price MUST be at least 1.3 times the hourly equivalent, computed as expected monthly hours times the freelancer's current hourly rate, and the rationale MUST show the three numbers (hours, rate, multiple). For an availability retainer the expected hours are the maximum monthly load, not the average. A retainer priced below 1.3x is rejected unless the rationale names the concession the client gave in exchange (12-month minimum term, prepayment of the full term).

rationale.source: This methodology's stated threshold (AGENTS.md: retainer rate at or above 1.3x hourly-equivalent); widely established freelance pricing practice

rule.rationale: A retainer sells the client two things an hourly contract does not: reserved capacity and priority. Selling those at the hourly price gives away the freelancer's only leverage and locks in the discount for the life of the engagement. The 1.3 floor is what keeps the "predictable income" story from becoming "20 percent pay cut for the same work".

rule.statement: The artefact MUST contain a written list of what the retainer includes, a written list of what it excludes (new-feature builds, emergency weekend work, third-party costs, meetings beyond a stated count), and a response-time or turnaround commitment in business hours or days. For block-of-hours the rollover rule (none, one period, capped at N hours) and the overage hourly rate MUST be stated; unused hours MUST NOT roll over indefinitely.

rationale.source: Widely established freelance contracting practice; Jonathan Stark on scope in productized services

rule.rationale: Every retainer dispute is a scope dispute: the client believes the monthly fee covers the new integration, the freelancer believes it covers maintenance. Written exclusions settle the argument before it starts. Uncapped rollover turns a quiet quarter into 90 banked hours the client can demand in one month, which is the availability risk the price never covered.

rule.statement: The retainer MUST state a minimum initial term of at least 3 months, a notice period of at least 30 days for either side, and a dated price-review point no later than 12 months from the start. The rationale MUST record these three dates or durations explicitly; "month-to-month, cancel any time" is rejected as a retainer shape.

rationale.source: Brennan Dunn, Double Your Freelancing Rate; widely established freelance contracting practice

rule.rationale: A retainer with no minimum term and no notice is hourly billing with extra steps: the client cancels the week the freelancer turned down other work to hold the capacity. The price-review date is what lets rates rise without a renegotiation being read as a betrayal; without it the retainer signed at 2024 rates is still running in 2027.

rule.statement: Each retainer period MUST be invoiced at or before the start of the period, with payment due before work in that period begins, and the artefact MUST state the billing day and payment terms. Retainers billed in arrears are rejected.

rationale.source: Jonathan Stark, Hourly Billing Is Nuts (2016); widely established practice in productized services

rule.rationale: Prepayment is the operational definition of a retainer: the client has retained the capacity. Billing in arrears re-creates the collections problem retainers exist to remove, and it means the freelancer carries the client's credit risk while also having reserved the hours. Every freelancer who has chased a 60-day-late retainer invoice knows which side of the invoice the leverage sits on.

rule.statement: When converting an existing hourly client, the artefact MUST show the client's average billed hours and spend over the last 3 months, set the retainer at or above 1.3x that spend under r-rate-floor-1-3x-hourly-equivalent, and name a cutover date after which hourly billing for the same scope stops. Running hourly and retainer billing in parallel for the same scope MUST NOT exceed one period.

rationale.source: This methodology's scope (AGENTS.md: phasing out hourly mid-relationship); Brennan Dunn, Double Your Freelancing Rate

rule.rationale: The 3-month average is the only number the client already accepts, so anchoring the retainer to it removes the "where did this price come from" objection. Parallel billing is how retainers quietly fail: the client keeps sending hourly tickets, the retainer hours go unused, and at renewal the retainer is cancelled as "not needed".

rule.statement: The artefact MUST list the freelancer's total committed monthly hours across all active retainers (using maximum load for availability retainers) next to the available billable hours, and the sum after adding this retainer MUST NOT exceed available hours. Signing a retainer that pushes committed hours over capacity is rejected until another retainer ends or is re-scoped.

rationale.source: Widely established practice in solo-consultancy capacity planning

rule.rationale: Retainers sell reserved capacity, and reserved capacity sold twice is a breach waiting for the month both clients call at once. Solo freelancers overselling availability is the most common way a retainer portfolio collapses: one missed turnaround commitment, one cancellation, and the "predictable income" disappears in the quarter it was needed.

rule.statement: The artefact MUST schedule an outcome review at 6 months from the start date and record, at that review: whether the retainer is still active without a renegotiation, actual hours delivered per period against paid hours, and the effective hourly rate realised. If actual hours exceed paid hours in 2 consecutive periods the review MUST produce a re-scope or a rate increase; if actual hours are below 50 percent of paid hours in 2 consecutive periods the review MUST address the client's usage before the client cancels.

rationale.source: This methodology's outcome-review criterion (AGENTS.md: retainer holds 6 or more months without renegotiation); Deming PDCA as applied to pricing review

rule.rationale: A retainer that quietly overruns is an hourly contract at a discount; one that is quietly underused is a cancellation notice in draft. Both are visible in the hours ledger months before they become a conversation, and the 6-month review is the point where the freelancer still has the leverage to fix either.

rule.statement: Run the full procedure; emit an artefact passing the output contract.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when the retainer signals hold.
